rationale: A wins because it knows when an angle is still conditional: “It survives only if merch is a material revenue line” and “Without the first item, do not pitch this” are the guardrails founders actually need. B has real bones, but it lets a shiny falsehood into the room with “Liquid Death's new store sells water you can't buy anywhere else — for now,” which is not in the update. That is not a polish problem; that is how a pitch becomes a correction.
gaps_in_A: “A brand present in roughly 120,000 retail doors has no distribution problem to solve” overstates the fact. Big distribution is not the same as no distribution problem.

“Liquid Death's first store is a merch shop that also sells water” is a sharp line, but it asserts a merch-first mix the update does not prove. A catches itself with the proof requirement, but the headline still gets ahead of the facts.
“The store opening gives a second reason to write about the company in the same window” is the thinnest bridge in the set. The B Corp angle stands on certification and donation proof, not the store.
gaps_in_B: “Liquid Death's new store sells water you can't buy anywhere else — for now” invents exclusivity. The update says limited-edition canned water, not store-exclusive water.
“near-total retail penetration” and “already everywhere” are lazy inflation. The update gives ~120,000 U.S. retail doors, not market saturation.
“a store-exclusive can is a different story” repeats the invented exclusivity and turns a limited edition into a product-pipeline signal without evidence.

“Next step: find-journalists” is premature. Close the proof gaps first, especially on exclusivity, profitability definitions, and B Corp documentation, or you are just building a media list for half-built stories.
